title: JRE 2224 - Tim Dillon
guestBio: This episode is brought to you by The Farmer's Dog. Get 50% off your first box by heading to http://thefarmersdog.com/rogan today!
tldr: Dillon's years working in mall retail and what they taught him about consumer culture, class, and the strange dignity and indignity of selling things to Americans for a living
Comedy and cowardice: Dillon's argument that apologizing for jokes is the worst thing a comedian can do and his contempt for the industry's increasing self-censorship
His unusual political profile - gay, economically heterodox, contemptuous of both woke orthodoxy and Republican messaging - and how that position gives him material that cuts in every direction
Dark comedy about American capitalism and wealth inequality: Dillon's bit of billionaire mythology, economic anxiety redirected into culture war, and the absurdity of late-stage consumer society
The mechanics of building a successful independent podcast outside the mainstream media infrastructure and what it means to own your audience rather than renting access from a platform
Conspiracy humor as its own genre: Dillon's approach to covering fringe theories comedically - taking them seriously enough to be funny without fully committing to any of them
recap:
Joe Rogan brings on Tim Dillon, comedian and host of The Tim Dillon Show, for a conversation that goes everywhere you'd want it to go and several places you wouldn't expect.

Dillon is genuinely hard to categorize politically, which is part of what makes him interesting. He's gay, Catholic by upbringing, economically left-leaning in some ways, contemptuous of liberal pieties in others, and absolutely merciless toward anyone who takes themselves too seriously. His comedy is rooted in a genuine bewilderment at how American capitalism works and a willingness to describe what he sees without pulling punches.

They spend a lot of time on his early life and the jobs he had before stand-up took off. Dillon worked at a mall for years - selling things, managing things, experiencing the full absurdity of consumer culture from the inside. He's a fantastic storyteller and his mall era stories are genuinely hilarious while also being incisive about class, work, and what happens to people when the economic floor disappears. Joe loves this kind of grounded material and lets him run.

Comedy and cancel culture overlap extensively. Dillon is loud about the cowardice he sees in his industry - comedians who apologize, clubs that self-censor, the general shrinking of what's permissible to say in public. He thinks the funniest material comes from places that are uncomfortable, and he's not interested in the alternative. Joe agrees, and they compare notes on what's happened to comedy since social media gave everyone a permanent record and an angry audience.

Wealth inequality is a recurring theme in Dillon's material and it comes up here. He has a darkly comic take on billionaire culture, the mythology of the American dream, and the way economic anxiety gets redirected into culture war. He's not ideological about it - he makes fun of socialist twitter with the same energy as hedge fund managers.

The conversation has the quality of two people who find the world deeply absurd and have made peace with that. Dillon is one of the funnier guests Joe has had in a while and this episode shows why his audience keeps growing.
